name: Morning height measurement trick

lead: People are slightly taller in the morning than in the evening, and the looksmaxxing 'morning height' practice is to measure or quote height just after getting out of bed to get the larger number. Forum users debate whether true height is the morning value, the evening value, or an average.

Research cited by Wikipedia found children's heights dropped by a mean of about 1.5 cm between waking and late afternoon. Clinical measurement guidance treats a wall-mounted stadiometer with standardised posture as the reference method.

paras: Spinal discs compress during upright activity and recover when lying down, so measured stature falls over the day and returns overnight. Posture, shoes, and measurement technique add further variation.

There are no meaningful health risks in measuring. The main caveat is measurement error: a typical error of about half a centimetre can make small real changes hard to detect, and self-reported heights tend to differ from measured values.

lead: The morning height measurement trick is the practice of measuring height shortly after waking, when it is at its daily maximum, instead of later in the day. It is discussed on height and looksmaxxing forums as a way to report a higher figure, to track results of height-related interventions consistently, or to decide what a person's 'real' height is [1][2].

Wikipedia reports that height changes over the day, that lying down for long periods tends to increase it and vigorous exercise before measuring tends to reduce it, and cites a study of 100 children whose heights fell by a mean of 1.54 cm between getting out of bed and mid-afternoon [3]. Clinical practice uses a stadiometer, a vertical ruler with a sliding headpiece, with the subject barefoot and standing erect against it [4].
Forum posters also discuss ways to keep morning height through the day, including supplements, core strength and insoles, claims for which no supporting studies were found [1].
infobox: About 1.5 cm lower by late afternoon [3]
Night height, true height, self-reported height

paras: Standing height is measured with a stadiometer in children over two and adults who can stand unaided; shorter or less mobile subjects are measured lying down or estimated with surrogates such as knee height, arm span or ulna length [3][5]. Wikipedia notes that measurement error is a limitation, and that a typical error of 0.5 cm can make small real growth look like negative growth or more than it is [3].

Grokipedia describes the reference measurement protocol as barefoot with heels, buttocks, shoulders and head against the backboard, and states that tape measures can add variability from sagging or inconsistent application [4]. A study of vertebral fractures reports that serial height measurement is used to monitor height loss in older adults [6].

A National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey analysis examined how age affects the validity of self-reported height, weight and body mass index [7]. Self-reported height is a different matter from the morning-versus-night question, but it is relevant because online discussions of the practice often involve what height a person states.

A thread titled around night versus morning height has a user reporting about 179.7 cm at night and about 181 cm in the morning and asking whether the average is his real height; replies agree the midpoint would be about 180.35 cm [2]. Another thread lists glucosamine, a stronger core and lower back, and heel insoles as things the poster says help maintain morning height through the day [1].

No studies found on the morning height measurement trick itself or on glucosamine, core training or insoles for retaining morning height. Related research includes the child study of diurnal height change cited by Wikipedia [3], measurement work on height loss in older adults [6], and studies of self-reported height [7].

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums, morning versus night height is a recurring question about which figure counts as a person's height.
